introduction-from-micro-to-macro.core: Individual postmortems fix individual incidents. Meta-analysis looks across many incidents to find systemic, organisational patterns (the iceberg below the surface) that no single review reveals.

first_principles.problem: Each postmortem concludes with a local fix, while the same underlying weakness (say, config changes) causes 40% of all incidents.

analogy.title: A hospital reviewing all deaths, not each one alone
analogy.story: Individually, each death had a cause; together they reveal that one ward is understaffed.
analogy.breaks: Meta-analysis needs enough incidents and consistent data to be meaningful.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: One systemic fix prevents dozens of incidents.

check.q: What can a meta-analysis reveal that single postmortems can't?
check.a: Recurring systemic patterns across many incidents, such as one class of change causing a large share of outages.

the-prerequisite-structured-metadata.core: Patterns need queryable data. Tag each incident with structured fields: severity, services, trigger type (deploy, config, dependency, capacity), detection method, contributing-factor categories and durations. Free-text documents can't be aggregated.

first_principles.problem: Hundreds of postmortems sit in unstructured Google Docs, so nobody can answer 'what triggers most incidents?'.
truths: Capturing at incident time is easiest.
derivation: **Capture** fields in the incident tool or a postmortem template.

analogy.title: Standardised medical coding
analogy.story: Diagnoses coded consistently (ICD codes) let researchers find trends across millions of records.
analogy.breaks: Too many fields cause sloppy entry, so keep the taxonomy focused.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 'Detection by customer' becomes a countable pattern.

code.text:
id: INC-412
severity: SEV2
services: [checkout, payments]
trigger: config_change
detection: customer_report
factors: [no_canary, missing_alert]
ttd_min: 34
ttm_min: 12

check.q: Why can't unstructured postmortems support meta-analysis?
check.a: Free text can't be reliably aggregated or queried for patterns.

pattern-hunting-common-organizational-sm.core: Meta-analysis diagnoses the organisation. Common smells: one team or service causing many incidents (ownership or debt), customer-detected incidents (monitoring gaps), Friday or deploy-related spikes (release process), repeat incidents (unfinished actions) and hero dependence.

first_principles.problem: Leadership sees incidents as random bad luck rather than symptoms of organisational issues.
derivation: **Change correlation**: incidents vs deploys or time of week.
**Repeat rate** and **action-item completion**; **hero analysis**: the same people every time.

analogy.title: A doctor spotting a pattern of symptoms
analogy.story: Fatigue, thirst and weight loss together point to a single underlying condition.
analogy.breaks: Correlation isn't causation, so investigate the clusters before acting.

steps.label: Actions
steps.detail: Modernise the service, improve monitoring, enforce action SLAs, spread knowledge.

check.q: What does a high percentage of customer-detected incidents indicate?

the-mttx-trap.core: Mean time metrics (MTTR, MTTD) look objective but mislead: incident durations are heavily skewed, so a few long ones dominate the mean, and the metrics are easy to game. Use distributions, percentiles and per-incident learning instead.

first_principles.problem: Leadership targets 'MTTR down 20%', and teams close incidents faster on paper while the real reliability doesn't change.

analogy.title: Average wealth in a bar when a billionaire walks in
analogy.story: The average jumps enormously, but nobody else got richer.
analogy.breaks: Trends in percentiles can still be useful, so the problem is naive means and targets.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: The mean measured luck, not improvement.

check.q: Why is MTTR often a misleading metric?
check.a: Incident durations are long-tailed, so a few outliers dominate the mean, and targets on it invite gaming.

presenting-meta-analysis-to-leadership.core: To drive investment, translate patterns into business terms: customer impact, revenue and engineering time lost, and risk. Then propose a few prioritised systemic investments with expected outcomes, rather than dumping charts.

first_principles.problem: Engineers present 40 charts of incident data, and leadership nods but funds nothing.
truths: Leaders allocate resources by business impact.
derivation: Start with the **headline**: '45% of SEV1/2 incidents come from config changes'.
Show the **cost**: customer minutes, revenue, engineering hours.
Make **2–3 concrete asks** with expected impact.

analogy.title: A doctor explaining test results to a patient
analogy.story: Not every lab value, but 'your blood pressure is high, here's the risk and here's the plan'.
analogy.breaks: Over-simplifying hides nuance, so keep the detailed appendix available.

example.title: A one-slide summary
flow: Headline: config changes caused 45% of major incidents
Ask: 2 engineers × 1 quarter for staged config rollout

check.q: What makes a meta-analysis presentation effective for leadership?
check.a: A clear headline pattern, its business cost, and a few concrete investment asks with expected outcomes.
